🚀 Full-stack developer interested in AI, space exploration, and NASA open data. Aiming to build an innovative prototype.

Seeking teammates skilled in frontend/backend, Python, AI/ML, data science, astronomy, GIS, or UI/UX. Beginners eager to learn are welcome!

Let's collaborate, innovate, and build something impactful for NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026! 🌙🛰️
summary:
Lunar Landing Site Navigator is a planning tool that compares south pole landing sites and dates by where the Sun and Earth sit against the real terrain horizon. It answers two questions a mission planner has: how much sunlight (power) and how much direct line of sight to Earth (communication) a site gets over a chosen window.

We built it on NASA data only: JPL Horizons for Sun and Earth positions, and LOLA elevation maps from NASA’s PGDA. A ray-casting engine follows the curve of the Moon out to 300 km in every direction to find the true skyline. The web app shows the sky, a horizon strip, local terrain, a time slider you can play, and a verdict with an uncertainty range. It also offers site comparison, a launch-slip matrix, a click-on-the-map site picker, and a public explainer.

It matters because at the pole the Sun skims the horizon, so a ridge can mean days of darkness or a lost Earth link. Where terrain data is incomplete, we say so: results are shown as an amber upper bound, never a false “viable”.
details:
What it does and how it works

Lunar Landing Site Navigator lets a mission planner, an educator or a member of the public compare lunar south pole landing sites and dates by where the Sun and the Earth appear against the real terrain horizon. It answers two practical questions: how much sunlight (power) a site gets, and how much direct line of sight to Earth (communication) it gets, over a window of 3 to 30 days between December 2026 and November 2029.

How it works, in four steps:

  1. Positions. Sun and Earth directions as seen from the site come from NASA JPL’s Horizons system.
  2. Terrain. NASA’s LOLA elevation maps (5 m site tiles, an 87S to 90S 5 m mosaic and a 20 m map, 14 GB in total) give the ground.
  3. Skyline. An engine casts 1,440 rays, one every quarter of a degree, out to 300 km, following the curve of the Moon, to find the highest ridge in every direction. That is the skyline a lander would see.
  4. Metrics. The tool computes sunlight, the longest dark spell, Earth link share and the longest outage. Each comes with an uncertainty range and a verdict against mission needs that the user can edit.

What you can do on the site:

  • A Command Centre shows the sky chart, a horizon strip, the local terrain in 2D and 3D, and the verdict on one screen. A time slider and Play button move the Sun and Earth across the window.
  • Compare puts 2 to 4 sites side by side. A slip matrix shows what happens if the start slips by 1, 3 or 7 days.
  • A site picker lets you click NASA’s polar map or type coordinates to build your own site.
  • An “Open in QuickMap” button opens the same site and time in NASA’s viewer for a cross-check.
  • A Public View tells the story in plain language, and a Spacecraft Dashboard compares a site with lander assumptions.

Benefits

  • It turns a hard geometry problem into numbers and pictures that a non-expert can read.
  • It lets a planner test many sites and dates in seconds, instead of one at a time in a general map viewer.
  • Every result shows where it came from, what was assumed and how uncertain it is.
  • It is free, open source (Apache-2.0), and runs in a browser with nothing to install.

Intended impact

We want better early decisions about where and when to land near the lunar south pole, where a ridge can mean days of darkness or a lost Earth link. We also want to help students and the public understand why the pole is hard. A clear tool lets more people take part in that conversation. It is a planning tool, not for flight operations, and it says so on every page.

Tools, languages, hardware and software

  • Data (NASA only): JPL Horizons API, NASA GSFC PGDA LOLA elevation products, NASA Moon Trek map tiles, LROC QuickMap links, NSSDC Apollo landing table, NASA CLPS list. Canadian Space Agency pages are linked in the Public View.
  • Engine and API: Python 3.12, NumPy and Numba, rasterio and pyproj, FastAPI, Pydantic, PostgreSQL, Redis, arq background jobs.
  • Web app: React 19, TypeScript, Vite, Tailwind CSS, OpenLayers and proj4 for the polar map, an OpenAPI-generated typed client.
  • Quality: pytest and Hypothesis (510 tests), Vitest (176 tests), Playwright (125 browser tests including accessibility checks with axe), mypy, ruff, GitHub Actions.
  • Hardware: one AWS EC2 server (Ubuntu) behind Caddy with HTTPS, running systemd services.
  • AI assistance: we used Claude (Anthropic) as an assistant for code, tests and documentation, under our direction. It is disclosed in the repository (docs/SI_USAGE.md). No AI runs inside the app, and no AI produces any calculated number.

How it is creative

  • It shows the terrain, not a flat horizon. The sky chart and horizon strip draw the real skyline with the Sun and Earth tracks, solid where visible and dashed where hidden by terrain.
  • It is honest about what it does not know. When NASA’s elevation data runs out before 300 km in some direction, the verdict is shown as an amber “upper bound”, never a false “viable”. We believe a tool for planning should refuse to flatter its own answer.
  • One shared clock drives every view, so the sky, the horizon, the terrain shading and the timeline always agree.
  • Layered explanation: a plain-language Public View, a guided Home page, and a definition under every metric.

Factors we considered

  • Accuracy and sources: only NASA data, with a recorded source and checksum for every file. We checked the Sun’s direction at six Apollo landing sites (five agree within 0.35°, Apollo 16 is off by 2.86° and we report that rather than tune it), and compared terrain heights and lit or shadowed areas with QuickMap.
  • Uncertainty: each result has a range from the elevation data’s own error. Terrain beyond the data is flagged and not guessed.
  • Reliability and security: rate limits, safe error messages, a dependency and secret scan, a backup restore test, and a tested rollback.
  • Accessibility: keyboard use, screen reader labels, contrast checks, and layouts that work down to a phone screen.
  • Performance: results are precomputed for the curated sites, and custom sites build in about a minute.
  • Transparency and fairness: data credits on a Credits page, every source with its usage terms, a clear AI disclosure, and a credit for every team member.

Known limits, stated openly: terrain reaches the full 300 km in only 46% to 95% of directions at the curated sites, so every verdict is an upper bound. The Earth link is line of sight only, with no antenna or radio model. The lander values are placeholders, and the QuickMap check was run by browser automation rather than by a person.

Links: live site https://13-52-97-105.sslip.io and code https://github.com/fury-05/nasa-lunar-landing-navigator-2026. Team: LunarOps (Irfan S. Mulla, Afreen Mulla, Luz Aponte).
